w: A 1950s flour mill on the Tyne, gutted and rebuilt in 2002 into one of Britain's biggest contemporary art spaces - no permanent collection, just a rotating churn of exhibitions. The rooftop restaurant and viewing platforms look across at the Millennium Bridge and the Sage, both born from the same 1990s push.
s: A flour mill turned into Gateshead's art powerhouse
_facts: Contemporary art centre on the south bank of the Tyne in Gateshead, no permanent exhibition, frequently changing shows
Opened July 2002 in a converted flour mill that had operated 1950-1984
Design by Dominic Williams of Ellis Williams Architects, who won a 1994 competition
Conceived in the 1990s alongside the Sage and Gateshead Millennium Bridge; over 8 million visitors by January 2022

w: Grade II listed and still doing exactly what it was built for - decades of touring musicians, classical programmes and standup comedy have passed through under whatever sponsor's name gets bolted on this year. Currently branded O2 City Hall; the building outlasts the branding every time.
s: Grade II listed, outlasting every sponsor's name
_facts: Concert hall in Newcastle upon Tyne, currently known as O2 City Hall Newcastle for sponsorship reasons
Has hosted popular music, classical artists, standup and comedy acts over the years
Operated by Academy Music Group, part-owned by Live Nation
Grade II listed building

w: Robert Stephenson's rail link toward Scotland, forged from 5,050 tons of iron and opened by Queen Victoria in 1849 - the same year the Mayor of Gateshead drove in its last key. A road deck was bolted on purely for extra revenue, and both still work: trains overhead, cars below under a weight limit, Grade I listed.
s: Stephenson's iron bridge, still carrying trains and cars
_facts: Road and railway bridge over the Tyne between Newcastle and Gateshead, built from 5,050 tons of iron by the Hawks family
George Hawks, Mayor of Gateshead, drove in the last key on 7 June 1849; opened by Queen Victoria later that year
Designed by Robert Stephenson to form a rail link to Scotland; a carriageway for road vehicles/pedestrians added for extra revenue
Still carries rail traffic and a weight-restricted road; Grade I listed structure

w: Augustus Welby Pugin's Gothic Revival cathedral, raised in just two years from 1842 and still the sixth-tallest structure in the city. Out front, the Monument Garden holds a memorial to Cardinal Basil Hume, opened by the Queen herself in 2002 - Pugin's spire watching over it, Grade I listed throughout.
s: Pugin's Gothic cathedral, built in just two years
_facts: Catholic cathedral, mother church of the Diocese of Hexham and Newcastle, on Clayton Street
Designed by Augustus Welby Pugin, built 1842-1844, Grade I listed, Gothic Revival style
Monument Garden outside holds a memorial to Cardinal Basil Hume, opened by Queen Elizabeth II in 2002
Sixth tallest structure in the city

w: 620 maisonettes fused into one unbroken block, designed by Ralph Erskine and built through the 1970s - one of British social housing's most recognisable silhouettes. The Wall itself is only the visible edge; the wider estate behind it sprawls across 200 acres of Byker.
_facts: Long unbroken block of 620 maisonettes in the Byker district, designed by Ralph Erskine, constructed in the 1970s
The Wall is part of a wider estate covering 200 acres in total

w: Grade I listed and sitting on Grey Street in the heart of the city - a historic theatre whose designation alone signals how much weight it carries architecturally. The facts on record are sparse, but the protection status speaks for itself.
s: Grade I listed theatre on Grey Street
_facts: Historic theatre, Grade I listed building, situated on Grey Street in Newcastle upon Tyne

w: Opened in 1904 on money from a local wine merchant, Alexander Laing, in a Baroque building with Art Nouveau flourishes - and stacked with heavyweights: Turner watercolours, Holman Hunt's 'Isabella and the Pot of Basil,' Burne-Jones's 'Laus Veneris,' even John Martin's apocalyptic 'Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah.'
s: A wine merchant's gallery, stacked with Turners
_facts: Art gallery on New Bridge Street West, designed in Baroque style with Art Nouveau elements by Cackett & Burns Dick, Grade II listed
Opened 1904, financed by a gift from local wine merchant Alexander Laing
Collection includes John Martin's The Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, Joshua Reynolds, Edward Burne-Jones's Laus Veneris, William Holman Hunt's Isabella and the Pot of Basil (1868), Ben Nicholson
Also holds 18th/19th-century watercolours by J.M.W. Turner and John Sell Cotman, plus Newcastle silver and Maling pottery
